results.summary: This design outputs ASCII-encoded text sequences character by character, selecting between two texts using a 2-bit input. One text is the beginning of a traditional Guatemalan song, and the other lists the project participants' names. An internal counter increments each clock cycle until a limit is reached, then resets to repeat the sequence. Testing requires an external microcontroller to read the 8 output pins synchronously and forward the characters over UART to a computer terminal; the author tested it with a TIVA C and an FPGA.

This project attempts to build a cascaded NOT-gate ring oscillator for delay measurements, but the synthesizer does not support combinatorial feedback and collapsed the cascaded inverters into buffers, so the original ring oscillator goal was not achieved. The two enable inputs control signal propagation through the gate chain to three output taps representing different gate stages. A square wave can be applied to the inputs and an oscilloscope used to measure stage delays for comparison with theoretical calculations. The design is presented as an educational experiment about synthesis limitations rather than a working oscillator.

This is an 8-bit wide, 128-byte ROM containing information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, with the first eight bytes holding the shuttle name in 7-segment encoding and the rest holding a null-terminated ASCII chip descriptor of key-value lines. The address is set on the eight input pins and the data is read from the eight output pins. The first bytes can be read by toggling the first four DIP switches and observing the on-board 7-segment display. The author's silicon test report states that the entire ROM was read back correctly.

This design implements JTAG test logic with four test data registers: an 8-bit boundary scan register between the fixed input and output pins, plus blink_in, blink_out and blink_dir registers for the two bidirectional pins. The JTAG TCK, TMS, TDI, TRSTn and TDO signals are routed through user IO, and the default clock and reset are left unconnected because JTAG supplies its own. It is controlled by resetting the core, shifting an instruction into the IR to select a TDR, then shifting data bits into that register. Testing requires a JTAG debug adapter, and the cocotb simulation includes helper routines for driving the JTAG state machine.

The project is titled "Later" and its one-line description, how-it-works and how-to-test sections all consist only of the word "Later". No functional description, pin names or test procedure are provided, so it is impossible to determine what the design does. The only concrete information is that it is a 1x1 Verilog tile with a 10 MHz clock. This appears to be an unfinished placeholder project with essentially no documentation.

This project is described in Spanish as a counter from 0 to 16 with load capability, implemented in Verilog. The pin names indicate a clock, reset, an initialisation or load input, an enable input, and outputs for a 7-segment display including segments b through g and the dot. However, the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are still the unfilled template text, so the exact counting behaviour, load mechanism and display encoding cannot be confirmed. The design is likely a simple educational counter driving a 7-segment display, but the documentation is too thin to describe it in detail.

This is a configurable PID control block intended to be configured over I2C, with six bidirectional GPIO pins used for error and control signals and two pins used as SDA and SCL. It also drives a 7-segment display through eight output pins. The description notes it was meant to be a final project but was undercut, and the how-to-test section refers to I2C files for the register addresses and an I2C test file for an example. The documentation is sparse and does not specify the PID parameters, fixed-point format or control loop details.

This is a serial vector graphics adapter that receives primitive drawing instructions over a UART at 921600 baud and drives X and Y outputs for an XY vector display. It has sixteen instruction registers that can be programmed and updated live over serial, with a state machine executing primitives such as lines and squares, and a safe/unsafe mode toggle plus a clock divider input for slow DAC drive speeds. The 8-bit X and Y outputs can be converted to analog with an R2R ladder or similar DAC arrangement, and the author tested it with a Teensy 4.1. External hardware needed includes two DACs, a vector graphics display such as an oscilloscope in XY mode, and a fast UART source.

This component computes the Collatz sequence for an 8-bit input number, using a four-register datapath and ALU that emulates basic assembler instructions driven by a simple state machine. Data is presented on the 8-bit input bus and the reset signal is activated to latch the input and begin the series calculation, with results appearing on the 8-bit output bus. The sequence is computed at close to the clock rate, so intermediate values are not visible without probing individual digital channels on an oscilloscope. The design is synchronous and includes a reset input, but the documentation gives no further detail on the instruction set or timing.

This design generates a PWM signal by comparing a selected duty-cycle bus against a counter, with the counter maximum resolution set by three bidirectional bit-selector pins. Higher resolution requires more counter bits and therefore produces a lower PWM frequency, and a D flip-flop on the comparator output synchronises the signal and reduces glitches when values change mid-run. The duty value is applied to the eight input pins and the PWM appears on the first output pin, with the maximum bits set on the bidirectional pins. Testing involves setting the duty bus and maximum bits, then pressing restart for the PWM to operate as configured.
